blocks.text: First separate **arthralgia** (pain, but the joint looks normal) from **arthritis** (objective swelling, effusion or deformity). Then decide whether the problem is **in the joint** (articular) or **around it** (periarticular: bursitis, tendinitis, enthesitis). The history, the joint involved, the **speed of onset**, and the patient’s age and sex all narrow the diagnosis.

blocks.title: History clues in a single hot joint
rows: Maximal within hours (6–12 h; gout often peaks in 2–6 h), wakes the patient early in the morning
Keeps getting worse over days until treated; fever
Diarrhoea or genital infection in the preceding weeks
Recent surgery, intercurrent illness or dehydration
New thiazide or loop diuretic; heavy beer intake
Large tense effusion soon after an injury, no skin change
Large effusion building up slowly without injury
Older age, RA, diabetes, immunosuppression, IV drug use, prosthesis, recent joint injection

blocks.title: Inflammatory vs mechanical pain
items: **Inflammatory:** worse after rest and better with use, **morning stiffness > 30 min**, warmth, swelling or redness.
**Mechanical:** worse with activity and relieved by rest (e.g., torn meniscus, OA).
Demographics: gout is commoner in men; inflammatory and autoimmune arthritis usually start before 50, OA mostly after 50.

blocks.title: Examination
items: Start with a **GALS screen**: watch the gait, squeeze across the MCPs and MTPs, feel each knee for warmth and effusion, rotate the hips, move the spine and neck.
Knee effusion: positive **bulge sign** and **patellar tap**. A ruptured Baker’s cyst can mimic a DVT; ultrasound sorts it out.
Periarticular problems (bursitis, tendinitis) typically hurt **more on active than passive** movement.
A septic joint is very painful and even tiny passive movements hurt; a **painless range of motion makes sepsis very unlikely**.
Look beyond the joint: fever, a skin portal of entry, pustules and tenosynovitis (disseminated gonococcal infection), conjunctivitis or balanitis (reactive arthritis).

blocks.text: Pattern helps: gout targets the **first MTP**, pseudogout the **knee and wrist** of older people, and reactive arthritis a **single lower-limb joint, usually the knee**.

Elderly, immunosuppressed and RA patients may have a septic joint with an **insidious onset and no fever**. About **20%** of septic arthritis involves more than one joint, so several hot joints do not rule it out.

blocks.note: Look at: the approach-to-arthritis algorithm, which splits articular from periarticular, inflammatory from non-inflammatory, and counts the joints involved.

blocks.text: Davidson ranks **crystal arthritis, sepsis, spondyloarthritis and oligoarticular JIA** as the key diagnoses in an acute monoarthritis. In a large joint, think OA, gout, pseudogout, trauma and septic arthritis first.

blocks.title: Causes of acute monoarthritis
rows: Gout; pseudogout (CPPD); septic arthritis; trauma and haemarthrosis; spondyloarthritis (reactive, psoriatic, enteropathic)
Psoriatic arthritis often presents in one joint
RA; juvenile idiopathic arthritis; gonococcal infection; tuberculosis; PVNS; foreign-body reaction; leukaemia and osteomyelitis (children)
RA seldom starts as a monoarthritis
Juxta-articular bone tumour; palindromic rheumatism; cholesterol crystals (chronic RA effusions); calcium oxalate (dialysis); plant thorn or sea-urchin spine
Thorn/spine reactions give a chronic monoarthritis or tenosynovitis
Lyme disease, brucellosis, fungi (Candida, mainly prosthetic joints); viral arthritis is usually polyarticular

blocks.title: Clues to specific causes
items: **Reactive arthritis:** acute arthritis of one lower-limb joint (often the knee) after gastroenteritis or an STI (Chlamydia commonest); HLA-B27 linked; the joint itself is sterile. Look for conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis and circinate balanitis.
**Gonococcal arthritis:** young, sexually active adult; migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis and pustules before the joint swells.

**Tuberculous arthritis:** about 1% of TB patients; hip, knee or spine; slow onset with fever, night sweats and weight loss. Fluid rarely shows bacilli, so synovial biopsy is needed; treatment runs 9 months.
**OA:** gradual onset and little swelling, unless a crystal flare is added; a cool, clear, viscous effusion.

blocks.text: In a **young adult with one acutely swollen joint**, think **gonococcal septic arthritis** until proven otherwise, even when urinary or genital symptoms suggest reactive arthritis.

Davidson and Kumar say RA **rarely** begins in a single joint; Pocket Medicine notes early RA can be monoarticular (knee, shoulder, wrist). In established RA, **one joint flaring out of step** with the rest is septic until the tap proves otherwise.

**Aspiration is mandatory** in acute monoarthritis, ideally before antibiotics. Send fluid for **Gram stain and culture**, **cell count**, and **compensated polarised light microscopy** on a fresh sample. Take blood cultures if sepsis is possible. Never put the needle through infected skin.

blocks.title: Synovial fluid categories
rows: Small volume, clear, straw-coloured, very viscous
Opaque, often frankly purulent, low viscosity
Trauma, bleeding disorder, PVNS, severe synovitis

blocks.title: Reading the tap at the bedside
items: Very cloudy: septic arthritis (occasionally gout).
Slightly cloudy or blood-stained, does not clot: pseudogout.
Frank blood that clots: haemarthrosis.
Unevenly blood-stained: the needle nicked the synovium.
**Fat layer floating on bloody fluid: intra-articular fracture** (marrow fat).
White fluid: heavy urate crystal load or cholesterol.

blocks.text: The tap is also **therapeutic**: draining a crystal effusion eases pain. Kumar injects steroid only if the fluid is clear or slightly cloudy; Davidson waits for **48 h of negative culture** before an intra-articular glucocorticoid when sepsis was suspected (not if TB is possible).

**Crystals do not exclude infection**: sepsis can coexist with gout or pseudogout, so always send Gram stain and culture. The Gram stain is positive in only about half of septic joints, and septic fluid can contain < 10 000 cells.

Books disagree on cell-count cut-offs: Davidson gives none, Kumar quotes septic fluid up to 75 000/mm³, and Pocket/Step-Up use > 50 000 with neutrophil predominance. The ranges overlap, so treat them as guides, not rules.

blocks.note: Look at: bright negatively birefringent urate needles (A) vs a few weakly positive pyrophosphate rhomboids (B).
Look at: urate needles and a small intracellular pyrophosphate crystal under polarised light with a red filter.
Look at: the joint aspiration technique (consent, sterile field, marked site, local anaesthetic).

blocks.text: Septic arthritis is the **fastest and most destructive** joint disease. Incidence is 2–10 per 100 000, rising to 30–70 per 100 000 with pre-existing joint disease or a joint replacement. Mortality is about **10%** (age is the main risk), and up to 50% when several joints are infected. Most cases follow **blood-borne spread** from a skin or upper respiratory infection.

blocks.title: Risk factors and presentation
items: Risk factors: older age, **RA** (macerated skin between deformed toes is a portal of entry), diabetes, immunosuppression, IV drug use, prosthetic joint, recent intra-articular steroid.
Hot, red, swollen joint with pain at rest and on movement, plus fever; **knee** then hip are commonest.
Over 80% are monoarticular; fever is present in only about 57%.
IV drug users get axial joints: sacroiliac, sternoclavicular, symphysis pubis.

blocks.title: Likely organism by setting
rows: Most adults, especially RA and diabetes
Gram-negative bacilli; group B, C and G streptococci

blocks.title: Investigations
items: **Joint aspiration** is pivotal (imaging-guided if deep). A **prosthetic joint is aspirated only in theatre**.
Synovial culture positive in about **90%**, Gram stain in only **50%**. Fluid is usually turbid or purulent; culture should cover gonococci and anaerobes.
Blood cultures positive in over half (about 80% if several joints).
Leucocytosis and raised ESR/CRP are usual but **may be absent** in the elderly, the immunocompromised, or early on. Serial CRP tracks the response.
**X-rays are of no value early** (normal for about 2 weeks); MRI/CT help for the hip.

blocks.title: Emergency management (Davidson Box 24.50)
rows: Aspirate for Gram stain and culture; blood cultures, FBC, ESR, CRP
**Flucloxacillin 2 g four times daily** (covers staphylococci and streptococci)
Clindamycin 450–600 mg four times daily (younger) or IV vancomycin (over 65)
Gentamicin 5 mg/kg once daily or vancomycin; avoid cephalosporins over 65 (C. difficile risk)
Serial needle aspiration to dryness 1–3 times daily; arthroscopic or open drainage if needed
Early passive movement, then active once pain and effusion settle
Traditionally 2 weeks IV, then 4 weeks oral
Orthopaedic team; removal is usually needed to clear infection

blocks.text: Regimens differ between books. Kumar & Clark Essentials pairs flucloxacillin with oral fusidic acid for 6 weeks, then one drug for 6 more; Zero to Finals uses flucloxacillin plus rifampicin for 3–6 weeks; US texts start vancomycin guided by Gram stain. For our exams, follow **Davidson: IV flucloxacillin 2 g QDS, 2 weeks IV then 4 weeks oral**.

**Gonococcal arthritis.** Disseminated infection occurs in up to 3% of untreated gonorrhoea: migratory arthralgia, low-grade fever, **tenosynovitis** and painful **pustules** (grey centre on a red base), then an oligo- or monoarthritis (knees > wrists > ankles). It is linked to terminal complement deficiency. Joint fluid grows the organism in only **30%**, so culture the **genital tract** (positive in 70–90%), throat and rectum; NAAT may be positive when cultures are not. Treat with **IV ceftriaxone** until better, plus a single oral dose of azithromycin (or a week of doxycycline).

blocks.title: Complications
items: Destruction of cartilage, ligaments and tendons, causing stiffness, pain and loss of function.
Avascular necrosis when the hip is infected; systemic sepsis and death.
Hip, wrist, elbow and ankle usually need **open** rather than arthroscopic drainage.

blocks.text: Suspected septic arthritis is an **emergency**: aspirate, then start IV antibiotics at once without waiting for culture results.

Classic patient: a middle-aged man woken by a **red, shiny, exquisitely tender first MTP joint** (podagra, over 50% of attacks). Pain peaks within **2–6 hours**; he cannot bear a sock or the bedsheet. Fever and even delirium can occur with large joints. Attacks resolve fully in **5–14 days**. The main differentials are septic arthritis, cellulitis and reactive arthritis.

blocks.title: Causes of hyperuricaemia and triggers
items: Over 90%: **reduced renal excretion** of urate.
Drugs: **thiazide and loop diuretics**, low-dose aspirin, ciclosporin, pyrazinamide.
CKD, alcohol (especially beer), lead poisoning, myeloproliferative disease.
Attack triggers: food or alcohol excess, dehydration, starting a diuretic.

blocks.title: Investigations
items: **Diagnosis = urate crystals** (needles, negative birefringence) in joint, bursa or tophus fluid; even a quiet joint between attacks may yield crystals.
**Serum urate can be normal during an attack** (up to 25% of measurements): recheck once it has settled.
ESR, CRP and neutrophils rise in the attack. Screen for metabolic syndrome: renal function, glucose, lipids.

X-ray is normal in acute gout. Chronic gout: **punched-out erosions** with sclerotic, overhanging edges and a preserved joint space; ultrasound **double-contour sign**; dual-energy CT separates urate from calcium.

blocks.title: Treating the acute attack (Davidson)
rows: Effective, but many patients have cardiovascular disease or CKD
Prednisolone 15–20 mg daily for 2–3 days (or IM methylprednisolone)
Once the diagnosis is clear and infection excluded
Aspirin (worsens gout), paracetamol alone (not anti-inflammatory), starting urate-lowering therapy mid-attack
**Keep taking it** and treat the attack

blocks.text: First-line drug differs by book: **Davidson = colchicine**; Kumar and Zero to Finals put a **high-dose NSAID** first (e.g. naproxen 750 mg then 500 mg 8–12-hourly), with colchicine or steroids if there is renal impairment or peptic ulcer; Pocket Medicine treats all three as equal. Pick by comorbidity; quote Davidson if asked for the first choice.

blocks.title: Urate-lowering therapy (ULT)
rows: More than one attack in 12 months, tophi, bone or joint damage, renal impairment, kidney stones. A single attack does not automatically need ULT
Xanthine oxidase inhibitor; start 100 mg daily (50 mg if elderly or renal impairment), raise by 100 mg every 4 weeks (50 mg steps if elderly or renal impairment) to target; max 900 mg/day
Colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily or an NSAID for the first few months; warn that flares are common and to **continue ULT through them**
Second line (allopurinol fails or is not tolerated); hepatic metabolism, no renal dose change
Usually lifelong, with yearly urate checks

blocks.text: Timing of ULT varies: Kumar says never start allopurinol within a month of an attack, and Step-Up says start it once the flare has settled. Davidson and Pocket Medicine both say **do not stop urate-lowering therapy** during a flare. Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (10–25% mortality) is linked to **HLA-B*58:01** (Han Chinese, Korean, Thai): screen these groups. Avoid allopurinol with azathioprine.

blocks.title: Chronic gout
items: **Tophi**: firm white urate nodules on fingers, elbows, Achilles tendon and ear helix; may ulcerate and discharge chalky material.
Kidney: urate stones and urate interstitial nephritis.

blocks.note: Look at: podagra, a swollen, red, very tender first MTP joint.
Look at: a tophus with white urate visible under the skin (diuretic-induced gout).
Look at: punched-out (“Lulworth Cove”) erosions at the first MTP joint in chronic gout.

blocks.text: Calcium pyrophosphate is deposited in cartilage, seen as **chondrocalcinosis** (linear calcification parallel to the joint surface). Chondrocalcinosis is rare under 55 but present in 10–15% of people aged 65–75 and 30–60% of those over 85. Acute **pseudogout** gives a warm, red joint with a large effusion, most often the **knee**, then the **wrist**; it is commoner in **elderly women**. **Fever and confusion are common.** Triggers: trauma, intercurrent illness, dehydration, surgery. Kumar calls CPP arthritis the third commonest inflammatory arthritis.

blocks.title: Associations and secondary causes
items: Common: **age and OA**.
Rare metabolic causes: **haemochromatosis, primary hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia**, hypophosphatasia, Wilson’s disease, familial forms.
Screen (calcium, magnesium, ferritin, PTH) if the patient is **under 25** or the disease is polyarticular; Davidson says **ruling out primary hyperparathyroidism is essential**.

blocks.title: Diagnosis
items: Aspirate: fluid often turbid, may be uniformly blood-stained or even look purulent.
**Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent** crystals on polarised microscopy.
X-ray: cartilage calcification and OA changes; **a normal X-ray does not exclude CPPD**.
Chronic forms mimic RA (“pseudo-RA”) or OA; deposits at C1–C2 cause **crowned dens syndrome**.

blocks.title: Management
items: Aspiration alone may settle it.
Persistent symptoms: **intra-articular glucocorticoid** (once sepsis is excluded), colchicine or an NSAID, used cautiously in the elderly.
Mobilise early. Asymptomatic chondrocalcinosis needs no treatment; chronic CPP arthropathy is managed like OA.

blocks.text: Exam classic: an older patient with **hypercalcaemia from primary hyperparathyroidism** develops an acute hot knee without fever. Expect **positively birefringent rhomboid** crystals.
**Sepsis and pseudogout can coexist**, and pseudogout itself causes fever and confusion. Always send Gram stain and culture, even when CPP crystals are seen.

blocks.note: Look at: calcified menisci and hyaline cartilage in the knee, with medial joint-space narrowing and osteophytes (CPPD on OA).

blocks.text: Haemarthrosis means bleeding into a joint. Causes: **trauma** (meniscal, cruciate or synovial tear, typically sports knee injuries; intra-articular fracture) and **bleeding disorders** (haemophilia, von Willebrand disease, sickle cell disease, warfarin). PVNS also gives a bloody effusion, but slowly.

blocks.title: Recognising it
items: Large effusion soon after injury, without periarticular swelling or skin change.
Aspirate: frank blood that clots, evenly blood-stained throughout.
**Fat globules floating on the blood = intra-articular fracture.**
Uneven staining that clears during the tap = a traumatic tap, not a haemarthrosis.

blocks.title: Haemophilia and the joints
rows: Spontaneous bleeds into joints and muscles
Bleeding after mild trauma or surgery
Excess bleeding only after major injury or surgery
Recurrent bleeds cause synovial hypertrophy, cartilage loss and chronic haemophilic arthropathy
Long APTT that corrects on mixing, low factor VIII, normal VWF

blocks.title: Acute haemophilic haemarthrosis
items: Give **factor VIII** (haemophilia A) or **factor IX** (haemophilia B) concentrate as early as possible.
Rest the joint with bed rest or a splint; ice packs.
Analgesia **without aspirin or NSAIDs**.
DDAVP helps only mild haemophilia A; it has no role in haemophilia B.
Once bleeding stops, mobilise and use physiotherapy to rebuild muscle strength; surgical decompression if severe.

blocks.text: Blood in the tap is not always a haemarthrosis: severe inflammatory synovitis, including pseudogout, can stain the fluid evenly. Still check for crystals and send Gram stain and culture.

cards.front: Speed of onset: crystal arthritis vs septic arthritis?
cards.back: Crystal arthritis peaks very fast (6–12 h); a septic joint builds up more slowly and keeps worsening until treated.

cards.front: How long must morning stiffness last to suggest inflammatory arthritis?
Davidson’s four most important causes of acute monoarthritis?
cards.back: Crystal arthritis, sepsis, spondyloarthritis and oligoarticular JIA.

cards.front: Which two conditions can present as monoarthritis in children?
Urate vs calcium pyrophosphate crystals under polarised light?
cards.back: Urate: needles, strongly negatively birefringent. CPP: rhomboids, weakly positively birefringent and sparse.

cards.front: Lipid layer floating on blood-stained joint fluid means…?
cards.back: Intra-articular fracture (marrow fat in the joint).
Normal < 3000/mm³; inflammatory > 3000; septic up to 75 000 (opaque, less viscous).

cards.front: Commonest organism in adult septic arthritis?
cards.back: Staphylococcus aureus (especially with RA or diabetes); gonococcus in young sexually active adults.

cards.front: Davidson’s empirical antibiotic and duration for septic arthritis?
cards.back: IV flucloxacillin 2 g four times daily (vancomycin if MRSA); traditionally 2 weeks IV then 4 weeks oral.

cards.front: Gonococcal arthritis: synovial vs genital culture yield?
Gout: joint, time to peak and duration of an attack?
cards.back: First MTP in over 50%; peaks in 2–6 h; resolves in 5–14 days.

cards.front: Does a normal serum urate exclude acute gout?
cards.back: No. Urate falls during inflammation; crystals confirm the diagnosis.
More than one attack in 12 months, tophi, joint or bone damage, renal impairment, nephrolithiasis.
100 mg daily (50 mg if elderly or renal impairment), raised by 100 mg (or 50 mg) every 4 weeks to target urate; max 900 mg/day; colchicine cover.

cards.front: When should pseudogout prompt a screen for secondary causes?
cards.back: Age under 25 or polyarticular disease; always rule out primary hyperparathyroidism.

cards.front: CPP crystals found in a hot knee aspirate. Is culture still needed?
cards.back: Yes. Sepsis and pseudogout can coexist.

cards.front: Factor VIII level in severe haemophilia and its joint consequence?
cards.back: < 0.01 U/mL; spontaneous haemarthroses leading to chronic haemophilic arthropathy.
Factor concentrate early, rest/splint and ice, analgesia without aspirin or NSAIDs, then physiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a painful, swollen right knee. She is stiff for about 90 minutes each morning, and the knee loosens up as she walks around the ward.
questions.leadIn: Which feature best indicates an inflammatory cause?
options: Prolonged morning stiffness that improves with use
Locking of the knee after twisting
questions.explanation: Inflammatory joint pain is worse after rest and better with movement, with **morning stiffness over 30 minutes**. Ninety minutes of stiffness easing with activity is the classic inflammatory pattern.
whyNot: Relief by rest is a mechanical feature.
Pain on loading (stairs) is mechanical.
Locking after a twist suggests a meniscal tear, a mechanical problem.
Crepitus points to OA, a non-inflammatory process.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old carpet fitter has a red, swollen area over the front of his knee. Passive flexion and extension of the knee are full and painless; resisted active movement is uncomfortable. Temperature 37.1 °C.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely type of problem?
questions.explanation: Pain on active more than passive movement points to a **periarticular** process such as bursitis. A painless passive range of motion makes septic arthritis very unlikely.
whyNot: A septic joint makes even small passive movements agonising.
Pseudogout is an intra-articular synovitis with a large effusion that limits passive movement.
A haemarthrosis gives a tense intra-articular effusion after injury.
Reactive arthritis inflames the joint itself, so passive movement would hurt.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has had a hot, swollen left knee for 4 days. Three weeks ago he had bloody diarrhoea after a barbecue. His eyes are red and gritty. The knee aspirate is sterile with no crystals.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An acute lower-limb monoarthritis weeks after gastroenteritis, with conjunctivitis and a **sterile** joint, is **reactive arthritis** (HLA-B27 linked).
whyNot: Gonococcal arthritis follows sexual exposure, often with pustules and tenosynovitis, and is not linked to diarrhoea.
No crystals were seen, and gout is unusual at 24 with this history.
RA rarely starts as a monoarthritis and does not follow diarrhoea or cause conjunctivitis.
TB arthritis is insidious over weeks to months with systemic symptoms.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has a swollen, painful right knee for a week. He is pale, has bruises on his shins and wakes at night with leg pain. Temperature 37.9 °C.
questions.leadIn: Which cause of monoarthritis must be excluded first?
questions.explanation: In children, **leukaemia** (and osteomyelitis) can present as a monoarthritis. Pallor, bruising and night bone pain are the warning features; a blood count is needed.
whyNot: JIA is a cause, but pallor and bruising point to marrow failure, which must be excluded first.
Gout is almost unknown in young children.
Pseudogout is a disease of older adults.
PVNS gives a slowly growing bloody effusion without pallor or bruising.

questions.stem: An 81-year-old woman has an acutely swollen right wrist. Polarised microscopy of the aspirate shows a few small rhomboid crystals with weak positive birefringence.
questions.leadIn: Which crystal has been identified?
questions.explanation: Sparse **rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent** crystals are calcium pyrophosphate (pseudogout).
whyNot: Urate crystals are needle-shaped, bright and negatively birefringent.
Cholesterol crystals occur in chronic RA effusions and make fluid look white.
Calcium oxalate is seen mainly in dialysis patients.
Basic calcium phosphate crystals are not identified this way.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old roofer slipped off a ladder; within an hour his left knee is tense and swollen. X-ray is awaited. Aspiration yields blood-stained fluid with a yellow oily layer floating on top.
questions.leadIn: What does the floating layer indicate?
questions.explanation: A **lipid layer on blood-stained fluid** is diagnostic of an **intra-articular fracture**: marrow fat has entered the joint.
whyNot: A traumatic tap gives uneven blood staining, not fat.
Septic fluid is turbid or purulent.
Haemophilic bleeding gives blood without fat.
PVNS gives evenly bloody fluid that builds up slowly, without fat.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man with diabetes has a hot, swollen left knee and temperature 38.6 °C. The aspirate is turbid; the Gram stain is pending. He has no drug allergies and no MRSA history.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, which empirical antibiotic should be started?
questions.explanation: Davidson’s first choice while cultures are awaited is **IV flucloxacillin 2 g four times daily**, which covers staphylococci and streptococci. Cephalosporins are avoided over 65 because of C. difficile.
whyNot: Cephalosporins carry a high C. difficile risk in patients over 65.
Oral therapy is not appropriate for initial treatment of a septic joint.
Fusidic acid is only an add-on in some regimens, never used alone.
Meropenem is not part of the empirical regimen.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old woman on prednisolone has had increasing pain in her right knee for 5 days. She is afebrile, her white cell count is normal and CRP is only mildly raised. The knee is warm with an effusion.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure, as normal blood tests exclude infection
Aspirate the knee for Gram stain, culture and crystals
Plain X-ray to look for septic changes
questions.explanation: In the elderly and immunosuppressed, fever, leucocytosis and a high CRP **may be absent**. Aspiration is mandatory in any acute monoarthritis.
whyNot: Normal bloods do not exclude sepsis in the elderly or immunosuppressed.
X-rays are normal early in septic arthritis.
Treating as gout before aspiration risks missing sepsis.
Steroid injection must wait until infection is excluded.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has had a red, exquisitely tender right first MTP joint since 4 a.m. Serum urate is 340 µmol/L (normal range).
questions.leadIn: What is the best way to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Repeat serum urate the next day
Aspirate and look for negatively birefringent needle crystals
questions.explanation: Serum urate falls during inflammation and is often **normal in an acute attack**. Gout is confirmed by **urate crystals** in joint fluid.
whyNot: Urate may stay normal during the attack; it is rechecked weeks later, not used to diagnose.
X-rays are normal in acute gout.
Blood cultures help if sepsis is suspected but do not confirm gout.
HLA-B27 relates to spondyloarthritis, not gout.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with tophaceous gout started allopurinol 3 weeks ago. He now has an acute attack in his left ankle and asks what to do with his tablets.
questions.leadIn: What is the best advice?
options: Stop allopurinol until the attack settles
Continue allopurinol and treat the attack
questions.explanation: Flares are common after starting urate-lowering therapy. Davidson says to **warn the patient and continue therapy** through an attack, treating the flare separately.
whyNot: Davidson says to warn about flares and continue therapy through them, not to stop it.
Doses are increased gradually, by 100 mg every 4 weeks.
Aspirin can worsen gout.
He has clear indications (tophi) for lifelong ULT.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman becomes confused and febrile 3 days after a hip replacement. Her right knee is hot and swollen. Knee X-ray shows linear calcification of the menisci.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An elderly woman, knee, a post-surgical trigger, fever and confusion, and **chondrocalcinosis** on X-ray all point to **pseudogout**. She still needs aspiration with culture.
whyNot: Gout usually affects the first MTP and the X-ray would not show chondrocalcinosis.
There is no preceding gut or genital infection.
RA rarely begins as an acute monoarthritis in old age.
There is no injury or bleeding disorder.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man has an acutely swollen knee and a temperature of 38.4 °C. The aspirate is turbid and shows CPP crystals.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Send the fluid for Gram stain and culture
questions.explanation: **Sepsis and pseudogout can coexist.** Finding CPP crystals does not exclude infection, so Gram stain and culture are always needed.
whyNot: Steroid injection before excluding infection could worsen a septic joint.
Allopurinol lowers urate and has no role in CPPD.
Discharge risks missing coexisting sepsis.
Urate is irrelevant once CPP crystals are seen.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with severe haemophilia A has a hot, swollen, painful right knee after a minor fall at school.
questions.leadIn: What is the most important first treatment?
questions.explanation: An acute haemarthrosis in haemophilia A needs **factor VIII concentrate** as early as possible, with rest, ice and analgesia that avoids NSAIDs and aspirin.
whyNot: NSAIDs worsen bleeding and are avoided.
DDAVP helps only mild haemophilia A, not severe disease.
Steroid injection does not stop bleeding.
Factor IX is for haemophilia B.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old footballer twisted his knee during a tackle. Within an hour it was tensely swollen. Aspiration yields frank blood that clots in the syringe; there is no fat layer.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Traumatic haemarthrosis from a ligament or meniscal tear
questions.explanation: Rapid swelling after injury with **frank blood that clots** is a haemarthrosis. In sports injuries it comes from torn cruciate ligaments or menisci.
whyNot: Septic fluid is turbid or purulent and develops over days.
Gout gives inflammatory fluid with urate crystals.
Reactive arthritis gives sterile inflammatory fluid weeks after an infection.
PVNS builds up gradually without a clear injury.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 67-year-old man on bendroflumethiazide for hypertension wakes at 5 a.m. with an exquisitely painful, red, shiny swelling of his left big-toe joint. He cannot bear the bedsheet on it.
items.explanation: Rapid early-morning onset at the **first MTP** in a man on a **thiazide** (reduced urate excretion) is gout.

items.stem: A 21-year-old woman has a hot, swollen right wrist with pain along the extensor tendons. Two days earlier she had flitting joint pains and now has a few painful pustules on her forearm.
items.explanation: Migratory arthralgia, **tenosynovitis** and **pustules** in a young adult are disseminated gonococcal infection.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man has a hot, swollen left knee, scaly plaques on his elbows and pitting of his fingernails. The aspirate is sterile with no crystals.
items.explanation: Step 1: sterile inflammatory monoarthritis. Step 2: skin plaques and nail pitting identify **psoriatic arthritis**, which often presents in one joint.

items.stem: A 70-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis for 20 years has had a rapidly worsening hot right knee for 3 days, out of step with his other joints. He has cracked, macerated skin between his toes.
items.explanation: Two steps: an RA joint flaring out of step with the others suggests sepsis, and skin breakdown between deformed toes is the portal of entry for **Staphylococcus aureus**.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Cholesterol crystal effusion of chronic RA

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman’s knee aspirate is cool, clear and highly viscous with a low cell count.
items.explanation: A cool, clear, viscous, low-cell effusion is **non-inflammatory**, typical of OA.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man’s knee aspirate is opaque and creamy, with 60 000 white cells/mm³, mostly neutrophils. No crystals are seen.
items.explanation: Opaque fluid with a very high neutrophil count and no crystals is **septic** until culture proves otherwise.

items.stem: A knee aspirate starts clear, then becomes streaked with blood as the needle is adjusted; the staining is patchy rather than uniform.
items.explanation: Uneven blood staining reflects the needle nicking the synovium: a **traumatic tap**, not a haemarthrosis.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has a turbid knee effusion containing long, bright needle-shaped crystals with negative birefringence.
items.explanation: Needle-shaped, **negatively birefringent** crystals are monosodium urate: gout.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with a known MRSA carrier status has a hot, swollen knee and fever. The aspirate is turbid and the Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
items.explanation: Step 1: this is septic arthritis, so empirical IV antibiotics start now. Step 2: Davidson uses flucloxacillin first-line, but **suspected MRSA (known carrier) means vancomycin** instead.

items.stem: A 23-year-old woman with fever, tenosynovitis and pustules on her hands now has a swollen knee. Cervical swab NAAT is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
items.explanation: Step 1: disseminated gonococcal infection with arthritis. Step 2: treatment is **IV ceftriaxone** until improvement, plus azithromycin or doxycycline.

items.stem: An 86-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 and a past peptic ulcer has an acute gout flare in several small joints of both feet, confirmed by crystals; infection has been excluded.
items.explanation: Step 1: NSAIDs are unsafe with CKD and an ulcer history, and colchicine toxicity is a concern in the elderly; with several small joints involved, injection is impractical. Step 2: Davidson recommends **short-course prednisolone (15–20 mg for 2–3 days)** as a good choice in older patients.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with CKD stage 4 has a hot knee. Fluid shows CPP crystals; Gram stain was negative and cultures remain sterile at 48 hours, but the effusion keeps reaccumulating. Colchicine and NSAIDs are to be avoided.
items.explanation: Step 1: crystals do not exclude sepsis, so cultures were awaited. Step 2: with **48 h of negative culture**, persistent pseudogout can be treated with an **intra-articular glucocorticoid**.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Joint aspiration for Gram stain, culture and polarised microscopy
Repeat serum urate after the attack settles
Aspiration in theatre by the orthopaedic team
Blood film and full blood count

items.stem: A 40-year-old man from Pakistan has had a swollen right hip for 3 months with night sweats and weight loss. Synovial fluid smear and culture are negative.
items.explanation: Insidious large-joint arthritis with systemic symptoms suggests **TB**. Mycobacteria are rarely found in fluid, so **synovial biopsy** is needed.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman has a hot, painful knee 5 years after a total knee replacement. Her CRP is raised.
items.explanation: Suspected prosthetic joint infection: Davidson says prosthetic joints should **only be aspirated in theatre**.

items.stem: A 22-year-old man has his second attack of acute knee pseudogout. He also has diabetes, bronzed skin and abnormal liver tests.
items.explanation: Step 1: pseudogout under 25 needs a screen for secondary causes. Step 2: diabetes, skin pigmentation and liver disease suggest **haemochromatosis**, so check ferritin and transferrin saturation.

items.stem: A 44-year-old man had a classic attack of podagra 4 weeks ago, confirmed by crystals; his urate during the attack was normal. He now wants to know whether he has hyperuricaemia.
items.explanation: Urate falls during an attack, so it is **rechecked weeks later**, once the inflammation has settled.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has a hot right knee 1 week after an infected leg ulcer. Fluid Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
items.explanation: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, diabetes and a skin source: **Staphylococcus aureus**, the commonest cause.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man had a hip replacement 14 months ago. He now has slowly increasing hip pain without fever; the prosthesis looks loose on X-ray.
items.explanation: Step 1: a delayed (3–24 month) prosthetic infection. Step 2: delayed infections are caused by low-virulence organisms such as **coagulase-negative staphylococci**.

items.stem: A 79-year-old man with recurrent urinary tract infections has a septic knee. The Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods.
items.explanation: Davidson: **Gram-negative bacilli** are important causes in the elderly; a urinary source and Gram-negative rods fit.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a new sexual partner has a hot, swollen left knee. The synovial fluid Gram stain shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci.
items.explanation: A young sexually active adult with **Gram-negative diplococci** has gonococcal septic arthritis.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has a swollen left knee with migratory joint pains, tenosynovitis of the wrist and a few painful pustules on her fingers. Knee fluid culture is negative.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation is most likely to identify the organism?
questions.explanation: In gonococcal arthritis, synovial culture is positive in only **30%**, whereas **genital tract culture** is positive in 70–90%. NAAT may be positive when cultures are negative.
whyNot: Synovial fluid grows gonococci in only about 30%, so repeating it is low-yield.
X-ray is normal early and does not identify organisms.
Urate is irrelevant to this infective picture.
ANA testing does not identify an organism.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man who moved from Somalia 2 years ago has had a swollen right knee for 4 months, with evening fevers and 6 kg weight loss. Repeated aspirates show inflammatory fluid with negative Gram stains and cultures.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Slow-onset large-joint monoarthritis with **constitutional symptoms** and sterile routine cultures suggests **TB**. Synovial biopsy and prolonged treatment are needed.
whyNot: Gonococcal arthritis is acute, with tenosynovitis and pustules.
Gout attacks resolve within 5–14 days.
Pseudogout is acute and affects older patients.
Reactive arthritis follows a gut or genital infection and does not cause weight loss over months.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 41-year-old man has recovered from his first ever attack of gout. He has no tophi, normal kidney function and no stones.
items.explanation: Davidson: a **single attack** does not necessarily need urate-lowering therapy. Indications are recurrent attacks, tophi, joint damage, renal impairment or stones.

items.stem: A 79-year-old woman with CKD has had three attacks of gout this year. Infection has been excluded and her current flare has settled.
items.explanation: Step 1: recurrent attacks are an indication for ULT. Step 2: in older patients and renal impairment, allopurinol starts at **50 mg daily**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has had several gout attacks despite allopurinol at the maximum dose he tolerated; his urate is still above target.
items.explanation: **Febuxostat** is used when allopurinol fails or is not tolerated.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with tophi who has taken allopurinol for 2 years presents with an acute flare of his ankle.
items.explanation: Never stop established allopurinol during an attack; **continue it** and treat the flare separately.

questions.leadIn: Choose the single best option for each patient. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 19-year-old student with a tremor, raised liver enzymes and brown rings at the edge of her corneas develops an acutely swollen knee. The aspirate contains weakly positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.
items.explanation: Step 1: pseudogout under 25 prompts a search for a metabolic cause. Step 2: tremor, liver disease and corneal rings suggest **Wilson’s disease**.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man on four-drug treatment for pulmonary TB develops sudden severe pain and redness of his big toe. Fluid shows negatively birefringent needles.
items.explanation: Gout during TB therapy: **pyrazinamide** reduces urate excretion.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman with kidney stones and a serum calcium of 2.9 mmol/L has an acute hot knee without fever. The aspirate shows CPP crystals.
items.explanation: Hypercalcaemia with stones and pseudogout: **primary hyperparathyroidism**, which Davidson says must be ruled out in pseudogout.

ospe.identify: Polarised light microscopy: **urate** = long needles with bright **negative** birefringence (gout); **calcium pyrophosphate** = few rhomboids with weak **positive** birefringence (pseudogout).
Red-filter polarised microscopy: needle-shaped **urate** crystals vs a small **pyrophosphate** crystal inside a white cell.
**Podagra**: swollen, red, very tender first MTP joint, the classic site of acute gout.
**Tophus**: white urate deposits visible under the skin (the white colour separates tophi from rheumatoid nodules).
**Chronic gout X-ray**: punched-out “Lulworth Cove” erosions with destructive arthritis of the first MTP joint.
**Chondrocalcinosis**: calcified menisci and hyaline cartilage in the knee, with joint-space narrowing and osteophytes (CPPD on OA).
